newsitem.title: UK: INSTANT VIEW - UK September RPI data.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - UK September RPI data.

text.p: Following is a selection of reactions to data showing UK headline retail price inflation (RPI) was +0.5% m/m and +2.1% y/y in September and underlying inflation (RPIX) was +0.5% m/m and +2.9% y/y:
The Reuters consensus forecast was 0.4% m/m and 2.0% y/y for RPI and 2.8% y/y for RPIX.

"We've clearly not got quite the balance that was expected. It seems as though there's been some attempt in some of the areas that have been experiencing quite strong growth in retail sales to push margins higher."

"I think the numbers are slightly negative for both short sterling and gilts. It confirms my view that underlying inflation has seen its bottom -- we may have 2.8 again, but we're basically still in a flat scenario, but most importantly above the government's target range. That counts out another cut in (interest) rates and does point to the next change being higher."
MARIAN BELL, ROYAL BANK OF SCOTLAND

"They're exactly in line with our own forecasts. I think it's consistent with a growing economy. We know that retailing is doing quite well and they've obviously used the opportunity to push through higher prices on the autumn lines at the end of the summer sales. I'm sure the chancellor still has a bias towards easing but the room for manoeuvre is extremely limited, especially if we get manufacturing picking up in line with the survey evidence."

"Increase in RPIX will come as a disappointment. While a jump in petrol prices was partly to blame, a number of other more representative categories also deteriorated. Household goods firm as were leisure services. Breakdown is still very mixed, with the likes of household services decelerating and fares and travel costs also lower. Not enough of a broad-based rise in the components to suggest that the bottom of the inflation cycle has been seen, but nonetheless ought to raise a few eyebrows at the BOE. Further reason for supposing base rate will not be cut again, unless the budget is surprisingly tight."
